questions.prompt: A fixed window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. What is its main weakness?
options: It needs a queue, which adds latency
Bursts at the window edge can let up to 2x the limit through, such as 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00
It uses a lot of memory per client
It can never reject a request
questions.explanation: The counter resets at each interval boundary, so traffic isn't smoothed and up to double the limit can slip through around the boundary. Sliding window fixes this.

questions.prompt: You need a strict, constant throughput to protect a fragile downstream system that can't handle spiky traffic. Which algorithm does the rule of thumb suggest?
options: Fixed window
Token bucket
Leaky bucket
Sliding window
questions.explanation: Leaky bucket processes requests at a constant outflow rate regardless of burst size. Token bucket is the common default because it tolerates bursts.

questions.prompt: How does `options.GlobalLimiter` differ from a named policy such as `AddTokenBucketLimiter("token", ...)`?
options: `GlobalLimiter` runs on every request automatically; a named policy applies only where it is attached with `.RequireRateLimiting` or `[EnableRateLimiting]`
`GlobalLimiter` only applies to anonymous requests
A named policy runs on every request; `GlobalLimiter` must be attached per endpoint
They are the same thing with different names
questions.explanation: The middleware checks `GlobalLimiter` unconditionally, in addition to any named policy the endpoint also has.

questions.prompt: Put the end-to-end flow of one request through the partitioned global limiter in order.
steps: The middleware calls the global limiter
The lambda checks `context.User.Identity` and picks the username or IP as the key
`PartitionedRateLimiter` looks up the bucket for that key, creating one only if the key is new
The request proceeds if a lease is acquired; otherwise, with `QueueLimit = 0`, it fails with 429
questions.explanation: The factory runs only the first time a key is seen; after that the same bucket instance and its remaining tokens are reused, which is what makes the limit per client.

source.section: Putting It Together — End-to-End Flow for One Request

questions.prompt: Each client gets a token bucket with `TokenLimit = 20`, `TokensPerPeriod = 5`, `ReplenishmentPeriod = 10s` and `QueueLimit = 0`. What does that allow?
options: Exactly 5 requests per 10 seconds, with no bursts
20 requests per second, queuing the rest
Unlimited requests, because `AutoReplenishment` refills instantly
A burst of up to 20, then about 0.5 requests per second, with rejection as soon as the bucket is empty
questions.explanation: The bucket holds 20 tokens and refills 5 every 10 seconds. `QueueLimit = 0` means no queuing, so an empty bucket rejects immediately.

questions.prompt: Your API runs as three instances behind a load balancer, using the built-in limiters. What is the problem, and the lesson's fix?
options: The built-in limiters refuse to start on more than one instance; switch to a fixed window
Limiter state is in memory, so each instance counts separately; use Redis-backed rate limiting as shared state
The load balancer resets all buckets; disable `AutoReplenishment`
There is no problem; instances share counters automatically
questions.explanation: Built-in limiter state doesn't sync across instances. A Redis-backed limiter such as `AddRedisTokenBucketLimiter` lets all instances see the same counters.
